paragraphs.heading: Three similar words
paragraphs.text: A seismometer usually works together with a timing device and a recording device, and the three form a seismograph. The output is a seismogram, which was formerly recorded on paper or film and is now recorded and processed digitally. The word seismograph is often used to mean seismometer. Both give a continuous record of ground motion. That record sets them apart from a seismoscope, which only shows that some motion has taken place.

paragraphs.heading: How modern instruments work
paragraphs.text: Early seismometers amplified the small motions involved with optical levers or mechanical linkages. Modern instruments use electronics. In some systems an electronic negative feedback loop holds the mass, as the weight is called, nearly motionless relative to the frame. The instrument measures how the mass moves relative to the frame. The feedback loop then pushes back with a magnetic or electrostatic force, which keeps the mass almost still. The seismometer gives as its output the voltage needed to make that force, and this is recorded digitally.

paragraphs.heading: Three directions
paragraphs.text: Seismic observatories usually have instruments that measure three axes: north-south, east–west and vertical. When just one axis is measured, the vertical is the usual choice. It has less noise, and it records some seismic waves better.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing the ground
paragraphs.text: For a seismic station, the foundation is critical. Professional stations are sometimes mounted on bedrock. The best place to mount one may be a deep borehole. Down there the instrument avoids thermal effects and ground noise, and also the tilting that weather and tides cause. Other instruments often sit in insulated enclosures, on small piers of unreinforced concrete that are buried. Before the pier is poured, a temporary installation is always used to survey the site for ground noise.

paragraphs.heading: The bronze dragons
paragraphs.text: Zhang Heng, of the Han dynasty in China, is said to have invented the first seismoscope in AD 132. The surviving description says it was a large vessel of bronze, about 2 meters across, with dragon heads at eight points around the top, each holding a bronze ball. When an earthquake came, one dragon mouth would open and let its ball fall into a bronze toad at the base. This made a sound and supposedly showed the direction of the earthquake. On at least one occasion the device indicated an earthquake even though none was felt. That was probably during a large earthquake in Gansu, in AD 143.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond Earth
paragraphs.text: The modern seismometer is a product of the 19th century. Starting in 1969, seismometers were placed on the Moon. They belonged to the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package. In December 2018 the InSight lander deployed a seismometer on Mars. It was the first time a seismometer had been placed on the surface of another planet.
